name: Aoki Lock from Aoki Lock Control
description: Aoki Lock from Aoki Lock Control uses the turned-out foot and hip connection to prepare a rotational finish. Protect the ankle and knee with early release.
target_area: Foot and ankle, with rotational stress transmitted to the knee
summary: The Aoki Lock is a rotational foot lock that captures a turned-out foot against the upper body while controlling the leg and hip, potentially stressing both the ankle and knee.
overview:
The attacker is seated or on a hip facing the opponent's leg, with the opposing foot turned outward beside the armpit and the hip connection controlled. The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.

Identify the turned-out foot without forcing it to rotate against resistance. Bring the instep under the upper arm and support the heel/Achilles region with the forearm. Secure the upper-body enclosure while leaving the foot unloaded during practice. Use the legs and hip connection to limit free movement without twisting a planted knee.

Use capture-and-release practice without finishing rotation. Pain is not a reliable warning margin for a secured rotational lock; neither partner should spin against a fixed foot.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Rob Biernacki — the Aoki lock](https://www.grapplearts.com/the-step-by-step-aoki-lock/); [IBJJF — current rule resources](https://ibjjf.com/books-videos).

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: which direction are the offered toes facing before you collect the foot?
flashcards.answer: Outward, away from the leg's neutral line. Identify an already outward-oriented foot rather than forcing a reluctant foot into the angle. The resulting enclosure can load both ankle and knee.
flashcards.answer_line: Outward from the neutral leg line

plausible: Straight up with no external turn
Inward across the opposite leg

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: which surface of the foot rests under your upper arm?
flashcards.answer: The instep against the biceps-and-armpit region. The instep meets the upper arm while the forearm supports the heel/Achilles region. Keep the capture unloaded in a control drill.
flashcards.answer_line: Instep at the biceps and armpit

plausible: Sole flat against your biceps
Only toes beneath your upper arm

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: where does Kesting place the looping hand for a deep arm connection?
flashcards.answer: Around the back of the opposite triceps. The written lesson distinguishes a deep hold behind the other upper arm from merely resting the hand on the biceps. Learn the connection without adding finishing rotation.

plausible: Lightly on the opposite biceps
Across their shin below the knee

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: what role do your legs play around the opponent's hip?
flashcards.answer: Limit free hip movement without twisting a planted knee. Use the legs and hip connection to limit free movement without twisting a planted knee.
flashcards.answer_line: Restrain hips without a knee twist

plausible: Replace the upper-body foot grip
Force a planted knee sideways
trap: Let hips retreat with toes caught

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: why is a large finishing motion unnecessary and hazardous?
flashcards.answer: Small body extension can load ankle and knee rotation. Recognize that a small body extension can create rotational ankle and knee pressure; do not search for a large finishing movement.

plausible: Load starts only with torso on mat
Calf squeezing absorbs extension
trap: Foot under arm keeps the knee safe

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: what must you open if the partner suddenly turns or taps?
flashcards.answer: Both the arm enclosure and the leg connection. Open the arms and leg connection on a tap, sudden turn, or loss of communication.

plausible: Outer hand, elbow still clamped
Free foot, hip still trapped
trap: Knees, while pulling the foot closer

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: which opposing post is collected in Kesting's counter-leglock example?
flashcards.answer: The foot pressing against the holder's hip. The example catches the foot that was pinning the defender's hip in standard ashi. A named dominant entanglement does not prevent that foot from being exposed.
flashcards.answer_line: The foot posted on the holder's hip

plausible: The knee on the mat behind them
The free heel outside both legs
trap: Toes tucked under their own hips

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: which mechanism distinguishes this from a calf slicer?
flashcards.answer: Rotation through an enclosed foot. The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.

plausible: Bent calf compressed over a fulcrum
Heel folded to same-side buttock
trap: Calf pressure with a free ankle

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: what amount of rotational load belongs in an initial capture-only repetition?
flashcards.answer: Contact without finishing tension through the leg. Rehearse collecting and completely releasing the foot and hip controls. Omit the finishing extension, and release if the partner moves or signals.

plausible: Tension to test remaining range
A small bridge before grip checks

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control: if the foot is not naturally presented at the right angle, what should you do?
flashcards.answer: Reset the entry instead of forcing the foot outward. Identify the turned-out foot without forcing it to rotate against resistance.
flashcards.answer_line: Reset instead of forcing the angle

plausible: Twist toes against a planted knee
Pull heel until the lower leg turns
trap: Fix knee and turn only the ankle

defender.description: Aoki Lock from Aoki Lock Control (defender): Treat an outward-turned foot caught by the upper body as a rotational lock rather than an ordinary straight ankle lock. Hand fight and recover foot position before the attacker connects around the foot.
defender.overview:
The attacker is seated or on a hip facing the opponent's leg, with the opposing foot turned outward beside the armpit and the hip connection controlled. The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.

Treat an outward-turned foot caught by the upper body as a rotational lock rather than an ordinary straight ankle lock. Hand fight and recover foot position before the attacker connects around the foot. Do not rotate the torso independently of a captured foot and knee.

Create slack in the hand and hip controls before withdrawing the leg. Stop at a secure rotational capture rather than testing whether the joint still tolerates movement. Wait for the entire enclosure to open before standing, turning, or restarting the exchange.

Use capture-and-release practice without finishing rotation. Pain is not a reliable warning margin for a secured rotational lock; neither partner should spin against a fixed foot.

Begin an escape while the hand enclosure and hip connection are still loose. Release the rotated-foot capture before bringing the freed knee back toward your torso; ordinary guard recovery starts after the ankle and knee can move together.

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control defense: what warns you that a straight-ankle response may be inadequate?
flashcards.answer: Your outward-turned foot is enclosed by their upper body. Treat an outward-turned foot caught by the upper body as a rotational lock rather than an ordinary straight ankle lock.
flashcards.answer_line: Turned-out foot clamped to the torso

plausible: Forearm touches only mid-calf
Ankle free beyond a loose elbow
trap: Hands on shin without foot contact

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control defense: before their grip closes, what should you contest?
flashcards.answer: The arm wrapping your foot while recovering its position. Hand fight and recover foot position before the attacker connects around the foot.
flashcards.answer_line: The wrapping arm; recover your foot

plausible: Their far ankle, your foot offered
Free knee, trapped leg pushed in
trap: The mat behind you with both hands

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control defense: why avoid turning your torso against a foot that remains fixed?
flashcards.answer: The turn can transfer load into the captured knee. Keep the torso from rotating independently of a foot and leg that remain restrained; have the full enclosure released before turning away.
flashcards.answer_line: The turn can load the trapped knee

plausible: It only tightens their forearm
The grip always follows harmlessly
trap: The foot turns freely in the clamp

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control defense: how does Kesting protect the outside foot while holding standard ashi?
flashcards.answer: Keep the inside knee close to that outside foot. His preventive detail closes access to the outside foot before an Aoki grip is established. It is not an escape to apply after the foot is already locked.
flashcards.answer_line: Keep inside knee near outside foot

plausible: Spread knees, expose the hip post
Turn toes away, leaving knee open
trap: Extend the post across their torso

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control defense: what is the problem with testing a secure lock for remaining movement?
flashcards.answer: Joint load may rise before pain provides a warning. Stop at a secure rotational capture rather than testing whether the joint still tolerates movement.
flashcards.answer_line: Joint load can precede the warning

plausible: Bent knees make rotation harmless
Only straight toes permit the lock
trap: A painless foot cannot load a knee

flashcards.question: Aoki from Control defense: what should be free before you stand or turn after release?
flashcards.answer: The entire foot enclosure and leg restraint. Wait for the entire enclosure to open before standing, turning, or restarting the exchange.
flashcards.answer_line: The foot clamp and leg restraint

plausible: Toes only, with heel still clamped
Hip only, foot beneath their arm
trap: Only one hand of the linked grip
